Family Health

Support pessaries for prolapse: fitting, care and follow-up

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A vaginal support pessary is a removable device that holds up prolapsed pelvic tissues and may ease a bulging or dragging sensation. It can offer an alternative to surgery or support you while waiting for another treatment. Success depends on a comfortable fit and a practical care plan. The device should help daily life without making urination, bowel movements or movement difficult.

A support device has a particular purpose

Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when the vaginal walls, uterus or top of the vagina descend from their usual position. A support pessary sits within the vagina to support these tissues. It is different from a dissolving vaginal medicine or a hormone-releasing ring, even though those products may also be called pessaries. Instructions for inserting a medicine do not describe care of a reusable support device.

Some designs may also help selected stress urinary leakage, such as leaking with coughing or exercise. A prolapse pessary does not necessarily resolve every bladder or bowel symptom, and supporting the prolapse can reveal leakage that was not obvious before. Tell the clinician which symptoms matter most so that fit and benefit can be assessed against your own goals.

Deciding whether to try one

A pessary can be considered at different ages, including when future pregnancy is planned, surgery is unwanted or an operation carries additional risks. It may be used for a short period or for ongoing symptom control. It supports the prolapse while in place rather than permanently repairing the tissues; symptoms may return when it is removed. There is no guaranteed two-year period free of surgery.

Discuss the alternatives, which may include observation for symptoms that do not trouble you, pelvic-health physiotherapy or surgery. The assessment also considers vaginal tissue health, previous pelvic treatment and whether removal and follow-up can be arranged reliably. Unexplained bleeding, active infection or significant tissue injury needs assessment before fitting; choosing a pessary should not delay that investigation.

Types and sizes are chosen individually

Many support pessaries are made of silicone or plastic. A ring, with or without an additional supporting membrane, is commonly tried first. Other options include a Gellhorn device with a stem, a cube or a donut shape. Their shapes affect how they provide support, how they are removed and whether they can remain in place during penetrative sex.

No one shape fits every person or every stage of prolapse. The clinician considers the examination, symptoms, comfort, sexual preferences and whether you want to manage removal yourself. A Gellhorn often needs clinic removal, while some rings are easier to self-manage. Inflatable devices are only one specific type; there is no universal instruction to inflate a pessary or position every design in the same way.

What a fitting appointment should establish

A trained practitioner explains the proposed vaginal examination and fitting and obtains your consent. You can ask for a chaperone, a pause or an end to the examination. Bring details of earlier prolapse treatment, medicines and any bleeding, discomfort or difficulties emptying. The first size may not be the final one: several attempts or appointments can be needed.

After fitting, you may be asked to walk, cough or change position to check comfort and retention. Make sure you can pass urine before leaving. Report pain, pressure or difficulty emptying rather than assuming you must get used to it. Obtain the name and size of the device, the planned review date and a contact for problems between visits.

Removal and clinic review are different schedules

Ask for separate instructions about removing and cleaning the device, replacing it with a new one, and attending a vaginal examination. Current UK guidance commonly starts with a review around four to six weeks after fitting and advises ongoing clinic-based follow-up no more than six months apart. Your team may arrange earlier checks according to symptoms, the device and tissue health.

People trained to self-manage may have a different clinic-review interval, but that does not mean leaving the device untouched until that appointment. Some devices need much more frequent removal; cube pessaries usually need daily removal and cleaning. Do not extend your own schedule to match a general six-month limit or another person’s longer review interval. If an appointment is missed or care becomes difficult, contact the service to agree a workable plan.

Self-management is an option, with training

Self-management means learning to remove, clean and replace your own fitted pessary and knowing when to ask for help. It can give more flexibility, but you do not have to choose it. Hand movement, reach, comfort, confidence and the device type all matter. Clinic care is a valid choice, and a change in health may mean revising an arrangement that previously worked.

Follow the technique you were taught for that device, with clean hands and any recommended lubricant. A water-based lubricant is often used, but confirm compatibility rather than adding oils or other products. Stop if removal or insertion is painful or meets resistance. Do not force it, improvise with tools or pull hard on a cube’s retrieval tail; ask the team for help.

Cleaning, storage and replacement

Use the manufacturer’s instructions and your clinic’s written plan. For many reusable devices, cleaning involves warm water and mild unperfumed soap, followed by thorough rinsing. If storing the pessary outside the body, follow the advice for drying it and keeping it in a clean container. Do not add disinfectants, harsh cleansers, boiling or another sterilising method unless the actual instructions require it.

Look for cracks, splitting, loss of flexibility or a change in shape, and report damage before using the device again. Discolouration alone does not always mean it needs replacing, while a device that no longer supports the prolapse may need reassessment even if it looks intact. A pessary is not automatically safe to use indefinitely because it can be washed. Cleaning the device also does not mean washing or douching inside the vagina.

Comfort, activity and sex

A well-fitting pessary should make ordinary activity more comfortable. Explain which movements cause symptoms, and ask for advice about exercise, lifting, coughing or constipation when relevant. Persistent pressure, pain or repeated slipping calls for a fit review. A device is not a reason to push through symptoms or a guarantee that every previous activity will immediately feel comfortable.

Penetrative sex is often possible with a ring in place if it is comfortable for everyone involved. Cube, donut and Gellhorn devices generally need a different plan because they occupy more vaginal space. Discuss this before choosing a device. If removal before sex is appropriate, use only the method and schedule you have been taught; do not assume that every type can be removed easily at home.

Vaginal dryness and prescribed estrogen

Thin or dry vaginal tissue can be more vulnerable to rubbing. A clinician may offer low-dose vaginal estrogen when appropriate, particularly with menopausal tissue changes, either before fitting or during use. It is a separate treatment decision, not something every pessary user must start. Explain your medical history, including previous breast cancer or unexplained bleeding, before using a hormone treatment.

Ask which preparation is intended, how to use it with your support device and when the tissue will be checked again. Follow the prescription rather than applying extra cream whenever discomfort occurs. Moisturisers or lubricants may be considered for selected symptoms, but pain, bleeding or a sore area still needs assessment. Hormone treatment does not remove the need for device care and follow-up.

Changes to report between appointments

A little extra discharge can occur with a pessary. An unpleasant smell, itching, pain, bleeding or a marked change in discharge warrants contact with the care team; these signs do not diagnose bacterial vaginosis by themselves. Vaginal rubbing or ulceration may require a break from the device, a different fit or other treatment. New bleeding, including after menopause, should be assessed rather than automatically blamed on the pessary.

If the device falls out, keep it safely and contact the team if you have not been taught what to do. Repeated expulsion needs a review; do not choose a larger size yourself. Report new leakage or trouble passing urine or stool. Get immediate medical help if you cannot pass urine at all or have severe pain or heavy bleeding. Do not wait for a routine appointment or persist with difficult removal.

Keeping treatment useful over time

At review, the team should ask whether the pessary helps, check its fit and examine the vaginal tissues as appropriate. Some people continue successfully for years; others change type, pause treatment or consider another option. Rare serious problems, such as a device becoming embedded or an abnormal opening into nearby organs, are reasons to take ongoing care seriously rather than assume every complication is minor.

Keep a brief record of the device name, removal plan, last examination and any symptoms. If you change clinics, share that information so responsibility for follow-up is clear. Ask for a review when the benefit changes, even if the next appointment is months away. The aim is sustained comfort and function with a plan you can actually follow.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask for the pessary name and size, a written removal and cleaning schedule, and a review date.

Discuss sexual preferences and self-management before choosing the device, and report changes in comfort or emptying.

Keep the service’s contact details and seek help between appointments when warning signs occur.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise device details, review dates and questions for your care team. It cannot choose a pessary size, examine vaginal tissue or replace professional fitting and urgent assessment.

When to seek help

Follow the instructions for your own support device. Do not force removal, use improvised tools or extend the removal interval to match someone else’s clinic schedule. Bleeding, pain, offensive discharge or new bladder and bowel difficulties needs advice; inability to pass urine at all, severe pain or heavy bleeding requires immediate medical help.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A support pessary is a fitted mechanical device, distinct from a vaginal medicine.
  • Comfort, retention and being able to pass urine are important checks after fitting.
  • Removal, cleaning, replacement and clinic review each need an individual written plan.
  • Self-management and penetrative sex depend on the device, training and comfort.
  • Report bleeding, pain or changed discharge; inability to pass urine requires immediate help.

Frequently asked questions

How should I care for a support pessary?

Use the cleaning and removal plan for your actual fitted device. Many reusable pessaries are washed with warm water and mild unperfumed soap and rinsed thoroughly, but frequency varies. Ask separately when the device needs replacing and when the vaginal tissues should be examined.

When should I contact the clinic?

Contact the team for bleeding, pain, offensive or changed discharge, repeated slipping, difficult removal or new bladder or bowel symptoms. Inability to pass urine at all, severe pain or heavy bleeding needs immediate medical help rather than waiting for the next appointment.

Why does a professional need to fit it?

An examination helps identify the prolapse, assess the tissue and choose a suitable shape and size. A poor fit can cause pressure, slipping or emptying problems. After fitting, some people can learn safe self-management; others prefer or need clinic care.

What side effects can occur?

Extra discharge, irritation, bleeding, slipping or changes in bladder and bowel function can occur. Some need a different fit or treatment. Serious complications are uncommon, but they should not be dismissed on the assumption that every device can simply be removed at home.

Can I leave it in until my next clinic appointment?

Only if that matches your individual removal instructions. A longer clinic-review interval for someone who self-manages is not permission to leave the pessary untouched. Cube devices usually need daily removal, and other products have their own schedules.

Can I have sex with it in place?

Often with a ring, if comfortable. Other designs can prevent comfortable penetration while in place. Discuss your preferences during fitting and agree whether removal is needed and whether you can do that safely yourself.

Will it cure the prolapse or prevent surgery permanently?

It supports the prolapse while in place and may help you avoid or delay surgery for as long as it remains useful. It does not guarantee permanent tissue repair or a fixed period without surgery. Treatment can be reconsidered as symptoms or preferences change.

Do I have to remove and replace it myself?

No. Ask about supported self-management if you want it, but clinic care is a reasonable alternative. The type of device and your comfort and ability matter. Arrange help promptly if your usual care becomes difficult.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
